items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My favorite story about that is the one that Phil Woods tells... Dizzy and Blakey – took me out to Dizzy’s home in Queens

ctx.x: We talked in the first part of the interview that we did yesterday. You mentioned Norman Mailer’s The White Negro. I’m wondering about your entry into the jazz world as a non-African-American and also about the usually unstated, but the endemic insecurity of a lot of white jazz musicians, that somehow they still feel that they have to be validated, in a sense accepted into the fraternity, to get that nod from the black player, in some sense.

My favorite story about that is the one that Phil Woods tells. He was still a young musician. He was at Birdland. In fact, insofar as people were writing about him, they would essentially say he was copying Charlie Parker. He was – as he puts it, he was whining one night. Dizzy Gillespie was there, and Blakey – Art Blakey was there. He said, “I’m not going anywhere. I’m white. I’m never going to make it.” So Phil said, “Then they kidnapped me. They put me in a car – Dizzy and Blakey – took me out to Dizzy’s home…
